extracted.intended_audience: educated readers interested in philosophy, ethics, and military history (readers of Montaigne)
extracted.subtask_description: A philosophical/reflective essay discussing the uncertainty of fame, prudence and conduct in war, horsemanship, and military prudence—mixing moral reflection with practical military observations and historical examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fame is uncertain and often arbitrary
rubrics_metrics.description: Reputation and glory rest on fragile signs—names, sounds, and accidents—rather than intrinsic virtue or lasting worth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and commentary: ‘Peter or William… what is it but a sound?’; anagrams (Nicholas Denisot); Suetonius changing Lenis to Tranquillus. Guidance: recognise fame as a transient echo or shadow of a dream rather than a secure good; beware valuing oneself by others’ flattery or nominal renown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh whether to press a victory or consolidate
rubrics_metrics.description: After a success, a commander must decide between pursuing advantage (to finish the war) and restraining ambition (to avoid overreach and disaster).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments for pursuit: finishing the war while the enemy is disordered; arguments against: risking over-extension and exposing oneself to fortune’s reversal. Historical examples: Moncontour, St. Quentin, Caesar reproaching Pompey; Monsieur de Foix at Ravenna vs Monsieur d’Anguien at Serisoles. Guidance: evaluate enemy condition, reserves, and your own capacity before continuing attack.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraint can be prudent—do not always drive an enemy to despair
rubrics_metrics.description: It may be wise not to pursue an utterly beaten foe to the last extremity because desperate enemies may fight with renewed ferocity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Sylla and Marius refrained when reserve forces appeared; Pharax allowed escaped Mantineans to go free to avoid encountering valour whetted by mischance. Anti-pattern: needlessly slaughtering or eliminating escape can create desperate resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leader visibility vs concealment: balance inspiring presence against personal risk
rubrics_metrics.description: A general’s conspicuous presence inspires troops but makes him the focus of enemy attacks; concealment preserves his life but may demoralise soldiers who rely on his example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Pyrrhus disguised under armour preserved himself but risked losing the battle; Alexander, Caesar, and Lucullus displayed conspicuous armour to be seen; Agis and Agesilaus fought obscurely. Guidance: weigh the morale effect on one’s troops against the strategic cost of losing the leader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose formation and motion tactically: charge or stand firm according to the enemy
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether to receive the enemy standing or to charge depends on enemy posture and the desired use of momentum and order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Debate: Pompey criticised for making troops stand to receive charge versus argument that a planted, steady posture is strongest. Practical rule given: ‘if your enemy come full drive upon you, stand firm to receive him; if he stand to receive you, run full drive upon him.’ Example: Clearchus’ timed sprint at fifty paces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer weapons you can control—favour short, reliable arms over unreliable missile devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose means of combat for which you can personally account; close weapons like swords are more dependable than complex missile arms requiring many contingencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text guidance: ‘choose weapons of the shortest sort, and such of which we are able to give the best account.’ Critique of early firearms: powder, wheel, and shot must all concur; swords allow more certain blows. Example: comparison of sword versus pistol reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foot combat yields steadier engagements; cavalry often produces routs
rubrics_metrics.description: Battles fought on foot tend to be firmer and more resolute; reliance on horses may produce more routing and less steadiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical note: ancestors fought on foot to rely on courage alone. Quotation: ‘They fought and fell pell-mell, victors and vanquished; nor was flight thought of by either.’ Guidance: favour infantry engagement when stability and mutual stake are desired; recognise modern cavalry-led tactics often lead to routs decided by first shout and charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trained aggressive horses are dangerous and can harm friends
rubrics_metrics.description: Horses trained to attack on command can be uncontrollable in melee, harming allies and being impossible to re-order once engaged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Artybius’ death when his horse, trained to grapple, exposed him and was killed; such horses may be useful but risk friendly casualties and loss of control. Anti-pattern: over-reliance on specially trained attacking horses without ways to recall or control them in chaos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Horse management and use of destriers: keep fresh mounts available
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of led or reserve horses (destriers) to change mounts in battle provides fresh stamina and enables feats of horsemanship; cavalry customs vary by people and purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Roman ‘desultorii equos’ and Numidian practice of holding a led horse; Parthians conducting many affairs on horseback; Bucephalus and Caesar’s famed horses. Practical guidance: keeping reserve mounts can sustain combat performance; training and discipline of horses are crucial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain logistical and territorial considerations when choosing where to fight
rubrics_metrics.description: Deciding to await an enemy at home versus attacking abroad involves tradeoffs in supplies, local support, risk of ravage, and strategic initiative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Points listed: defending home offers supplies, friendly population, river/passes, and fortified cities; invading gives opportunity to spoil enemy lands and may be advantageous. Examples: Scipio chose to attack in Africa successfully; Hannibal erred by leaving foreign gains to defend home; Athenians failing in Sicily vs Agathocles succeeding in Africa. Guidance: weigh supply lines, population reaction, and ability to sustain wounded and wounded-lodging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seize or deny enemy resources to prevent mutiny—remove arms and horses from recently conquered peoples
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent rebellion among newly subjugated peoples, commanders often disarm them and take horses as a security measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited Caesar practice: ‘Arma proferri, jumenta produci, obsides dari jubet.’ Guidance: early measures after conquest should include depriving potential rebels of arms and mounts to secure occupation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the moral and psychological effects of missile and siege weapons
rubrics_metrics.description: Missile arms, incendiary javelins (Phalarica), slings, and siege engines have both physical destructive power and significant effects on morale and fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Phalarica that fly like lightning; slingers practised to hit small targets; engines at Syracuse analogous to modern artillery. Note cultural differences: Gauls disdain such treacherous missile arms preferring hand-to-hand glory. Guidance: select weapons not only for physical effect but for their influence on morale and cultural acceptance of soldiers.
